t:
(a) In General.—Section 2302(b)(8) of title 5, United States Code, is amended—
        (1) in subparagraph (A)(i), by striking “a violation” and inserting “any violation”; and 
        (2) in subparagraph (B)(i), by striking “a violation” and inserting “any violation (other than a violation of this section)”.  
    (b) Prohibited Personnel Practices Under Section 2302(b)(9).—
        (1) Technical and conforming amendments.—Title 5, United States Code, is amended—
            (A) in subsections (a)(3), (b)(4)(A), and (b)(4)(B)(i) of section 1214 and in subsections (a), (e)(1), and (i) of section 1221, by inserting “or section 2302(b)(9) (A)(i), (B), (C), or (D)” after “section 2302(b)(8)” each place it appears; and 
            (B) in section 2302(a)(2)(C)(i), by inserting “or section 2302(b)(9) (A)(i), (B), (C), or (D)” after “(b)(8)”.  
        (2) Other references.—
            (A) Title 5, United States Code, is amended in subsection (b)(4)(B)(i) of section 1214 and in subsection (e)(1) of section 1221 by inserting “or protected activity” after “disclosure” each place it appears. 
            (B) Section 2302(b)(9) of title 5, United States Code, is amended—
                (i) by striking subparagraph (A) and inserting the following:
“(A) the exercise of any appeal, complaint, or grievance right granted by any law, rule, or regulation—“(i) with regard to remedying a violation of paragraph (8); or“(ii) other than with regard to remedying a violation of paragraph (8);”; and 
                (ii) in subparagraph (B), by inserting “(i) or (ii)” after “subparagraph (A)”.  
            (C) Section 2302 of title 5, United States Code, is amended by adding at the end the following:“(f)(1) A disclosure shall not be excluded from subsection (b)(8) because—“(A) the disclosure was made to a supervisor or to a person who participated in an activity that the employee or applicant reasonably believed to be covered by subsection (b)(8)(A)(i) and (ii);“(B) the disclosure revealed information that had been previously disclosed;“(C) of the employee’s or applicant’s motive for making the disclosure;“(D) the disclosure was not made in writing;“(E) the disclosure was made while the employee was off duty; or“(F) of the amount of time which has passed since the occurrence of the events described in the disclosure.“(2) If a disclosure is made during the normal course of duties of an employee, the disclosure shall not be excluded from subsection (b)(8) if any employee who has authority to take, direct others to take, recommend, or approve any personnel action with respect to the employee making the disclosure, took, failed to take, or threatened to take or fail to take a personnel action with respect to that employee in reprisal for the disclosure.”.

fable.w: The tempting reading is that the words "participated" and "appeal, complaint, or grievance right", plus the amendments to sections 1214 and 1221, signal outside-party participation or a right to sue. But the section only broadens the definition of protected whistleblower disclosures and prohibited personnel practices for federal employees and applicants. Any remedy is an individual appeal of a personnel action against that person, not consultation with outsiders on a federal policy decision. It creates no comment period, hearing, advisory body, rulemaking, or consultation with states, tribes, or the public.
fable.s: the disclosure was made to a supervisor or to a person who participated in an activity that the employee or applicant reasonably believed to be covered by subsection (b)(8)(A)(i) and (ii)

opus.w: These amendments change which whistleblower disclosures and protected activities count as prohibited-personnel-practice violations for federal employees. They also make conforming changes to the existing appeal provisions. The people involved are mostly federal employees challenging reprisals against themselves, which is an individual grievance like the manufacturer's appeal in Example 11. No outside party is brought into a federal policy decision. The mention of appeal rights is tempting, but it neither opens a federal decision to outside participation nor gives the public a new right to sue over a policy.
opus.s: “(A) the exercise of any appeal, complaint, or grievance right granted by any law, rule, or regulation—“(i) with regard to remedying a violation of paragraph (8); or“(ii) other than with regard to remedying a violation of paragraph (8);”
opus.b:
**Tempting reading:** The section extends whistleblower protections, mentions "any appeal, complaint, or grievance right," and amends 5 U.S.C. 1214 and 1221 (the Office of Special Counsel and individual-right-of-action appeal provisions). That looks like giving someone a right to challenge a federal decision.

**Why it fails:** The people protected are mainly federal employees, who are inside the federal government. What they challenge is a reprisal personnel action against them as individuals, not a federal policy decision. That is closer to the individual appeal in Example 11 than to outside parties taking part in a decision. "Applicant" could cover someone outside government, which is why my confidence is moderate.

qwen_chat.w: This section defines prohibited personnel practices related to whistleblower protections and internal grievance procedures for federal employees. The interactions described (disclosures to supervisors, appeals, grievances) occur entirely within the federal government between employees and their superiors or agencies. There is no requirement for the federal government to consult or coordinate with parties outside the government (such as the public, states, or private entities) before making a decision.
qwen_chat.s: (A) the exercise of any appeal, complaint, or grievance right granted by any law, rule, or regulation—“(i) with regard to remedying a violation of paragraph (8); or“(ii) other than with regard to remedying a violation of paragraph (8);”
qwen_chat.b:
Temptation: It looks like participation because it refers to "the exercise of any appeal, complaint, or grievance right" and disclosures to supervisors.
Resolution: These are internal administrative procedures for federal employees to report misconduct or appeal personnel actions. The actors involved (employees, supervisors, the agency) are all inside the federal government. There is no consultation with or participation by outside parties (public, states, tribes, etc.) in a federal decision-making process.
